In Agile, there are several ways to order items in the Product Backlog. Understanding ways to order work is essential as it will guide the overall sequence in which items are developed and delivered.

The value of ordering is to maximize return on investment (ROI) of the Product Backlog. So the Product Owner and stakeholders collaboratively order the Product Backlog, reviewing the ROIs for various chunks of work to be done. They also take into consideration:

  • Risks mitigated by completing certain work (e.g. creating prototypes, draft versions or proofs of concept)
  • Dependencies between Backlog Items such as:
    • A can only be completed once B is done
    • C will be easier to complete once D is finished
  • Potential changes in needs, requirements or market landscape
    • Elements more prone to changes might be developed first to learn more about them and better fit them to stakeholders' needs
    • Alternatively, the Product Owner might decide to postpone the riskier items so that the impact of change is minimized
  • Contractual, market and internal conditions - every development initiative is set in a certain environment, which influences the order in which work should be done (e.g. to meet regulatory requirements or release a new product during a particular window in the market)

A few of the most common supplementary ordering techniques include:

MoSCoW Method - which allows Agile practitioners to sort User Stories, features or Epics into distinct categories that inform the relative priority for each. The categories for MoSCoW are:

  • Must have - indicating essential items which are critical to success
  • Should have - designates items that are very important but not critical to successful delivery
  • Could have - defines those items that are desired but will not have as significant of an impact if left out as leaving out "Should have" items
  • Won't have (or sometimes Would like to have) - specifies items that may be incorporated if time allows

This technique can only be used as a preliminary step toward an ordered Product Backlog as it produces groupings of elements, which still require more detailed ordering within each category.

To employ the MoSCow technique, define the meaning of each category. It is important that individuals understand the overall objectives of the initiative, the MoSCoW categories and how to exercise discipline when selecting assignments (e.g. there can be a tendency to assign most requirements to the "Must have" category).

Once the initial Product Backlog is complete and the MoSCoW category definitions understood, gather the relevant group of stakeholders to agree on the relative importance of each item. Note, these categorizations can be changed later as part of backlog grooming as ordering is an ongoing effort.

MoSCoW provides more clarity than simply designating High, Medium or Low importance as it conveys the relative significance of not delivering a specific set of items. For example, if there is a feature that without which the initiative would not deliver its objectives, this would need to be designated as a "Must have".

Buy a Feature - Engages stakeholders in a group setting, allowing them to influence the ordering or, and assign relative importance to, items in the Product Backlog.

To employ the Buy a Feature technique, assign prices to all of the items in the Product Backlog. Ideally, use a fictional currency, such as Monopoly dollars, to avoid participants confusing prices with cost to develop. Existing estimates such as story points can be used and scaled, if needed, to expedite the price assignment process. Otherwise, it is recommended that the estimate, complexity and risk related to the feature are reflected in the price. Note that pricing with a high degree of precision is not the key point of the exercise, quickly defining the relative price should be the focus. Planning Poker or Affinity Estimation are often used to quickly determine prices for Backlog Items.

Next, allocate a budget to each participant, the amount of money allocated to each person may, but does not necessarily need to, vary to reflect their:

  • Importance to the project, product or company and/or
  • Relative seniority or experiences

The overall budget available must be less than the overall total for all features to force decision making and it should be made clear that budgets can remain unspent if features do not justify their costs.

There are two approaches that can be taken to employ the Buy a Feature technique:

  • Collaborative Buy a Feature - where participants are encouraged and expected to collaborate, including pooling their money together, to buy an expensive feature. Encourage participants to discuss and influence each other, so that common understanding of the entire group's needs can be achieved. This exercise is best done in a face to face workshop or via screen sharing and video conferencing. The approach places focus on the stakeholder group in order to obtain more accurate insights on what is truly needed and valued. This helps the single Product Owner who may have valid, but potentially limited, information to better understand the opinions of the broader group. To increase the likelihood of collaboration, the sum of all budgets should not exceed 50-75% of the sum of all feature prices.
  • Non-collaborative Buy a Feature - all participants buy features on their own so collaboration is not necessary although conversations may be allowed to occur. With each purchase, participants should explain the rationale behind purchasing a particular feature. The facilitator should capture these explanations so that they can be used to better understand the stakeholders' needs. The results of this exercise, including how often a feature was purchased and supporting rationale, are used as the input for ordering. The budget for each participant in this scenario should be limited to no more than 20-40% of the sum of all feature prices.

Regardless of the approach, the participants use their budget to purchase the items they value the most.

Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF) - is intended to facilitate the ordering of Product Backlog items by giving preference to those that provide the most value for the least amount of development time. It is based on a simple metric:

WSJF = Value / Cost

Where:

  • Value represents the value achieved when a certain part of the product is completed
  • Cost represents the total cost of completing that same part of the product

Typically, for Backlog Items cost is approximated by using their associated estimates (e.g. story points). To estimate value, discuss and agree with the stakeholders on a certain scale of value. For example, some common scales include:

  • 1-5: where 1 is low, 3 is medium, and 5 is high
  • Fibonacci series of relative value: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, etc.
  • Powers of 2 series: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, etc.

Next, use estimation techniques such as Planning Poker or Affinity Estimation to work with stakeholders and arrive at the relative value sizing for each item.

Divide the value of each item by cost of each item to arrive at a weighted value. Arrange items in decreasing WSJF order to arrive at a proposed order.
